assessment:
In this study, Kudryashev and colleagues present the first three-dimensional structures of Yersinia enterocolitica and Shigella flexneri injectisomes in their native cellular environment using cryo-electron tomography. The injectisome is a critical virulence factor in Gram-negative bacterial pathogens, functioning as a molecular syringe to inject effector proteins into host cells. While previous structural studies had characterized isolated injectisome basal bodies from Salmonella and Shigella, this work provides the first in situ structural analysis of these complexes within intact bacteria, revealing unexpected features of their architecture and mechanical properties.

The authors employ an integrative structural biology approach combining cryo-ET at 4 nm resolution for Y. enterocolitica and 7 nm for S. flexneri, X-ray crystallography of the YscD component at 1.4-2.7 Å resolution, molecular dynamics simulations, and integrative modeling. The key findings include: (1) basal bodies show 20% length variation (30-36 nm intermembrane distance) within bacterial populations, (2) in situ structures are approximately 10 nm (~40%) longer than isolated structures, (3) the YscD protein exhibits tertiary structure elasticity allowing ~3.5 nm elongation with minimal force resistance, and (4) the secretin YscC is stretched by 30-40% in situ compared to its liposome-reconstituted state. These observations are validated through osmotic stress experiments showing that high salt conditions induce statistically significant (~10%) elongation of basal bodies. The authors construct a pseudo-atomic model of the YscDJ inner membrane ring using particle swarm optimization constrained by experimental data, proposing a 24-meric assembly where elongated YscD conformations best fit the cryo-ET density.

The evidence supporting the main structural claims is solid, with appropriate resolution estimates, independent validation through CEMOVIS imaging, and functional validation of the G283P YscD mutant. The molecular dynamics simulations convincingly demonstrate YscD's ability to transition between compact and extended conformations with barrier-free elasticity, and the steered MD quantifies the mechanical properties. However, some aspects remain tentative: the assignment of cytoplasmic components (YscV/YscN) relies on analogy to flagellar motors rather than direct identification, the exact stoichiometry of the rings is inferred rather than definitively proven, and the functional significance of the observed elasticity, while plausible, remains speculative. The authors appropriately acknowledge these limitations and the resolution constraints of their cryo-ET maps.

This work makes an important contribution to understanding bacterial secretion systems by revealing that injectisomes possess intrinsic structural flexibility that may allow them to accommodate variations in periplasmic space dimensions. The finding that two-membrane-spanning complexes can exhibit such elasticity through tertiary structure rearrangements has broader implications for understanding how macromolecular assemblies cope with mechanical stress. The study exemplifies the power of integrative structural biology, combining multiple techniques to overcome the limitations of any single approach. While the functional importance of elasticity and its generality to other systems require further investigation, the structural observations are robust and the mechanistic insights into YscD flexibility are well-supported by multiple lines of evidence.
